title: Koko has piles of bananas and h hours before the guards return. Each hour she eats up to a chosen speed k bananas from one pile. Find the minimum integer speed k such that she can finish all piles within h hours. Run in logarithmic time over the speed.
shortTitle: Koko Eating Bananas — Binary Search on the Answer With a Feasibility Check

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Koko Eating Bananas is the canonical binary-search-on-the-answer problem. Instead of searching an array, we binary-search the space of possible eating speeds, using a feasibility function that computes the hours needed at a given speed. Because feasibility is monotonic, faster speeds never need more hours, we can binary-search for the smallest feasible speed in O(n log m) time, where m is the maximum pile size.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The bank must clear a backlog of transaction batches before a deadline. It can set a processing rate, how many items per hour each worker handles. A higher rate clears the backlog faster. The manager binary-searches the rate: pick a middle rate, compute whether the backlog clears in time, and if it does, try a lower rate to save resources; if not, raise the rate.

**One line to remember:** Binary-search the answer itself, using a yes-or-no feasibility check that is monotonic.

sections.s2_technical:
When the answer lies in a numeric range and feasibility is monotonic, we binary-search the range instead of an array. Here the answer is the eating speed, which ranges from 1 to the largest pile.

The feasibility function computes hours needed at a speed k. For each pile, the hours are the pile size divided by k rounded up, because a partial pile still costs a full hour. We compute the ceiling without floating point using `(pile + k - 1) / k`, then sum over all piles. Feasible means that sum is less than or equal to h.

The monotonic property is the whole justification: if speed k finishes in time, any speed greater than k also finishes in time, and if k is too slow, any smaller speed is also too slow. This yes-then-no boundary is exactly what binary search locates.

The search is a lower-bound pattern over speeds: `int low = 1, high = max(piles); while (low < high) { int mid = low + (high - low) / 2; if (canFinish(piles, mid, h)) high = mid; else low = mid + 1; } return low;`. On a feasible mid we try smaller by setting high to mid; on an infeasible mid we must go faster by setting low to mid plus one. When they meet, low is the minimum feasible speed.

A senior-level nuance is the ceiling-division trick to avoid floating-point error and to stay exact, which matters because a rounding mistake would miscount hours. Another nuance is bounding the search correctly: the minimum useful speed is 1 and the maximum useful speed is the largest pile, since eating faster than the largest pile gives no further benefit.

The pattern generalizes to many optimization questions, which is why it is a staple: whenever you can phrase a problem as find the smallest or largest value for which a monotonic condition holds, binary search on the answer applies.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India has several batches of pending transactions that must all be cleared before a regulatory cutoff a fixed number of hours away. The bank can provision a processing rate, items per hour per batch, but higher rates cost more compute, so it wants the minimum rate that still meets the deadline. This maps exactly onto Koko Eating Bananas, where piles are batches, the deadline is h hours, and the eating speed is the processing rate.

Problem 2 — Trying every possible rate one by one would be slow, but the feasibility condition is monotonic, a faster rate never needs more hours, so we binary-search the rate and compute hours needed at each candidate rate.

Problem 3 — Hours per batch must be a ceiling, because a leftover partial batch still consumes a whole hour slot, so we use exact integer ceiling division to avoid rounding errors in a compliance-critical deadline.

In the code: a `RateOptimizer` holds the batch sizes and the deadline. A `minRate` method binary-searches the rate using a `hoursNeeded` feasibility helper. A `RateDemo` main finds the minimum rate for a set of batches.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: batches 30, 110, 230, 100, deadline 5 hours. The maximum batch is 230, so rates range from 1 to 230.

Step 1: low 1, high 230, mid 115. Hours needed: 30 over 115 is 1, 110 over 115 is 1, 230 over 115 is 2, 100 over 115 is 1, total 5, which is at most 5. Feasible, so try slower, high becomes 115.

Step 2: low 1, high 115, mid 58. Hours: ceil 30/58 is 1, ceil 110/58 is 2, ceil 230/58 is 4, ceil 100/58 is 2, total 9, greater than 5. Infeasible, go faster, low becomes 59.

Step 3: The window keeps narrowing between 59 and 115, each step computing hours and moving the bound, until low equals high at the smallest rate whose total hours is at most 5.

Step 4: For this input the minimum feasible rate converges to 115, because at 115 the total is exactly 5 and at 114 the 230 batch would need 3 hours, pushing the total to 6.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26 22:40:00 [INFO] Finding minimum processing rate to clear batches before cutoff
2026-10-26 22:40:00 [INFO] Minimum rate -> 115 items/hour per batch
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: batches [30 110 230 100], deadline h=5
  Search space: rate in [1 .. 230]
    │
    ▼ binary search on rate (monotonic feasibility)
  mid=115 → hours=5 ≤ 5 feasible → high=115
  mid=58  → hours=9 > 5 infeasible → low=59
  ... converge ...
  low==high==115
    │
    ▼
  Output: minimum feasible rate = 115 items/hour
```

```
  │   RateOptimizer                       │
  │  + minRate(batches, h): int           │ O(n log m)
  │  - canFinish(batches, rate, h): bool  │ monotonic predicate
  │    uses ceil = (b + rate - 1) / rate   │ exact integer
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  Call chain:
  1. minRate(batches, 5)
  2.   low=1 high=max(batches)
  3.   loop: canFinish(mid)? high=mid : low=mid+1
  4.   return low (minimum feasible rate)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Koko Eating Bananas is the textbook example of binary search on the answer, which is a technique I reach for whenever the answer is a number in a known range and there is a monotonic yes-or-no condition on that number. Instead of searching through an array, I search through the space of possible eating speeds. The feasibility function computes how many hours Koko needs at a given speed by summing, over every pile, the ceiling of the pile size divided by the speed, because a leftover partial pile still costs a full hour. Feasible means that total is within the hour budget.

The entire approach rests on monotonicity: if a given speed finishes in time, every faster speed also finishes in time, and if a speed is too slow, every slower speed is also too slow. That yes-then-no boundary is precisely what binary search pinpoints. So I run a lower-bound search over speeds, and whenever a candidate speed is feasible I try to go slower by pulling the high bound down, and whenever it is infeasible I must go faster by raising the low bound, converging on the smallest workable speed in time proportional to n times log of the maximum pile.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this to pick the minimum processing rate that still clears all pending transaction batches before a regulatory cutoff. The batches are the piles, the cutoff is the hour budget, and the processing rate is the eating speed, where a higher rate costs more compute, so finding the minimum feasible rate directly saves money.

Two details matter in production. First, I compute hours per batch with exact integer ceiling division, using pile plus rate minus one divided by rate, to avoid any floating-point rounding error that could miscount hours before a compliance deadline. Second, I bound the search between a speed of one and the largest batch, because provisioning faster than the largest batch gives no further benefit. The real value of mastering this is that the same template solves a whole family of optimization problems just by swapping the feasibility check.
